q: What is the time complexity of the brute-force closest-pair method for n points?
What is the running time of the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm with presorting?
explain: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), solved like merge sort. Without presorting by y, the strip must be sorted at every level, which gives O(n log² n).

q: After solving both halves (closest distance δ), which pairs still need checking?
options: Only pairs with one point on each side, both within δ of the dividing line
Every pair in the left half again
All pairs in the whole set
Only the two points next to the line
explain: Any pair closer than δ must cross the line, and a point further than δ from the line is too far from everything on the other side.

q: In the strip (sorted by y), with how many following points must each point be compared, at most?
explain: A δ × 2δ box can contain at most 8 points that are pairwise at least δ apart, so only the next 7 by y can be closer than δ.

q: How wide is the strip that is checked around the dividing line?
explain: A crossing pair closer than δ has both points within δ of the line, on their respective sides.

q: The strip can contain Θ(n) points, yet the strip check still takes only O(n) time.
explain: True. Each strip point is compared with at most 7 neighbours, giving O(7n) = O(n), even when every point lies in the strip.

q: For the points (2,3), (12,30), (40,50), (5,1), (12,10), (3,4), which pair is closest?
explain: Their distance is √(1 + 1) ≈ 1.414. The next candidate, (2,3)–(5,1), is √13 ≈ 3.6.

q: What is the base case of the recursion?
options: 2 or 3 points, solved by brute force
explain: With very few points, checking all pairs directly is cheapest. One point has no pair at all.

q: Why are the points presorted by x?
options: So each split into left and right halves is just taking the first and second halves of the list
explain: With the points sorted by x, the dividing line and the halves come from the middle index in O(1).

q: In one dimension (points on a line), what is the simplest way to find the closest pair?
options: Sort the points and check consecutive pairs: O(n log n)
Divide and conquer with a strip
explain: On a line, the closest pair must be neighbours in sorted order.
